diagram_classification: cosmological (wind rose / twelve-wind diagram, with a possible computistical or temporal reading)
interpretation: A wheel diagram with a human head in profile at the centre. Twelve radiating lines run from the central roundel to the outer circle, each ending in a triangular knotwork (triquetra-like) terminal. The pattern most likely represents the twelve winds arranged around the earth, or around the microcosm (man) at the centre of the cosmos. The head stands for the human being as microcosm, or for the earth or world placed at the centre of the universe. The twelve rays and terminals stand for the twelve winds, in the tradition of the wind rose, which is often paired with the twelve months or the twelve zodiac signs. The alternating yellow and blue-grey terminals probably mark the winds' qualities or the hot/cold and wet/dry opposition between them. The outer orange ring is the boundary of the cosmos or firmament. The text above the diagram is only partly visible and cannot be read reliably.
evidence: Visible: a central roundel with a ringed human head in profile; twelve radiating lines of unequal length ending in triangular knotwork terminals; colours alternating between yellow and blue-grey; a thick orange outer circle; a few partly legible lines of Latin text above. The twelve-fold division and the radial layout are typical of medieval wind diagrams and of man-as-microcosm schemes. External knowledge: Isidore of Seville (De natura rerum) describes twelve winds, and early medieval manuscripts, including Insular and Carolingian ones, illustrate them with wheels or with a human figure at the centre. The knotwork terminals point to an Insular or Insular-influenced milieu. The exact identification, whether winds, months or another twelve-fold series, cannot be confirmed because no labels are legible, so certainty is limited.
